llm_reflection.explanation: Round-003 tested the previous hypothesis that CP-SAT at max_seconds=3 would either improve the F_competition incumbent below 63.0 s or return OPTIMAL at or below 63.0 s. The result falsified the improvement/optimality part of the hypothesis: the solver again returned FEASIBLE at exactly 63.0 s, with the same best bound of 51.0 s, the same 12.0 s absolute gap (19.0% relative), and the same verified makespan. The candidate was verified (independent replay valid, zero constraint violations, zero deadlock) but was not accepted because it produced no lexicographic improvement over the round-002 incumbent. This is a meaningful negative result: tripling the CP-SAT budget from 1 s to 3 s increased branches from 34890 to 37268 and conflicts from 5780 to 5780 (unchanged), yet the incumbent and bound did not move at all. That strongly suggests the 1 s run had already reached a local plateau for this model encoding, and that the remaining 12.0 s gap is not closable by simply adding more time to the same formulation. The verified metrics also reveal the structural reason: RINSE processing is 28.0 s (the nominal bottleneck), but chamber blocking is 45.0 s total (CLEAN 19.0, ALT 19.0, RINSE 7.0), and robot utilization is 0.698 during the completion window. The makespan of 63.0 s is therefore dominated by robot transfer serialization and chamber blocking, not by raw chamber processing load. The nominal RINSE lower bound of 28.0 s is far below the achieved 63.0 s, confirming that the bottleneck is the single-gripper robot schedule, not chamber capacity. Cost-wise, round-003 consumed about 4.28 s wall and 3.58 s skill time for zero improvement, a cost ratio of about 2.04x the incumbent's tool time, so further blind CP budget increases on this scenario are poor value. The next cheapest informative probe is a different search method on the same scenario: an RL policy evaluation using an allowed pretrained model, which explores a different region of the schedule space than the exact CP encoding and may escape the plateau. If RL also fails to beat 63.0 s, that would strengthen the case that 63.0 s is near-optimal for this instance and that effort should shift to the untried G_dual_bottleneck scenario.
llm_reflection.failure_explanation: Round-003 did not fail verification: the simulation completed, independent replay was valid, and there were zero constraint violations and zero deadlocks. It failed only the acceptance criterion of lexicographic improvement, because the CP-SAT search at 3 s returned the same FEASIBLE makespan of 63.0 s and the same best bound of 51.0 s as the 1 s run. The hypothesis that additional CP search time would either improve the incumbent or certify optimality was falsified. The likely cause is that the CP model's search plateaued: the incumbent hint from round-002 was reused, branches increased only modestly (34890 to 37268), and the bound did not tighten, indicating the remaining gap is structural to the model encoding rather than a matter of search time. The 12.0 s gap to the bound therefore remains open and is not evidence that 63.0 s is optimal.
llm_reflection.testable_hypothesis: On F_competition, an RL policy evaluation using an allowed pretrained model (medium-seed-0) will return a verified complete-batch Makespan different from 63.0 s, because the CP-SAT plateau at 63.0 s across 1 s and 3 s budgets indicates the exact encoding is stuck in a local region, and a learned policy explores a different schedule space; if RL also returns 63.0 s or worse, that would support treating 63.0 s as near-optimal for this instance and shifting effort to G_dual_bottleneck.
